name: Two permutations
description: You are given two permutations p and q , consisting of n elements, and m queries of the form: l 1 , r 1 , l 2 , r 2 ( l 1 ≤ r 1 ; l 2 ≤ r 2 ) . The response for the query is the number of such integers from 1 to n , that their position in the first permutation is in segment [ l 1 , r 1 ] (borders included), and position in the second permutation is in segment [ l 2 , r 2 ] (borders included too). A permutation of n elements is the sequence of n distinct integers, each not less than 1 and not greater than n . Position of number v (1 ≤ v ≤ n ) in permutation g 1 , g 2 , ..., g n is such number i , that g i = v .
input_specification: The first line contains one integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10 6 ) , the number of elements in both permutations. The following line contains n integers, separated with spaces: p 1 , p 2 , ..., p n (1 ≤ p i ≤ n ) . These are elements of the first permutation. The next line contains the second permutation q 1 , q 2 , ..., q n in same format. The following line contains an integer m (1 ≤ m ≤ 2·10 5 ) , that is the number of queries. The following m lines contain descriptions of queries one in a line. The description of the i -th query consists of four integers: a , b , c , d (1 ≤ a , b , c , d ≤ n ) . Query parameters l 1 , r 1 , l 2 , r 2 are obtained from the numbers a , b , c , d using the following algorithm: Introduce variable x . If it is the first query, then the variable equals 0 , else it equals the response for the previous query plus one. Introduce function f ( z ) = (( z - 1 + x ) mod n ) + 1 . Suppose l 1 = min ( f ( a ), f ( b )), r 1 = max ( f ( a ), f ( b )), l 2 = min ( f ( c ), f ( d )), r 2 = max ( f ( c ), f ( d )) .
output_specification: Print a response for each query in a separate line.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 323C — Two permutations [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
